newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin under friendly pressure on privatisation.
newsitem.headline: Jospin under friendly pressure on privatisation.

text.p: French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin came under friendly pressure on Monday to go ahead with privatisation plans frozen when his Socialist-led government took office this month.

Former Communist transport minister Charles Fiterman, who quit the party in the early 1990s and is now an independent leftist, added his voice to a call made by Socialist former European Commission president Jacques Delors on Sunday night.
Delors told Europe 1 radio that he favoured "opening up the capital" of France Telecom so that "this magnificent group, one of the five biggest in the world ...can forge all types of alliances".
He also said staff at troubled flag carrier Air France "can only be made to understand the nature of competition today if the company is privatised".

Pilots and ground staff at Air France and its domestic unit, Air Inter Europe, have staged repeated strikes against management efforts to bring salaries and working conditions of new recruits into line with those at other airlines.

Jospin said in his keynote policy speech to parliament last week he did not favour privatisation of the telecommunications, electronics and aerospace sectors, "in the absence of a justification drawn from the national interest".
But he left himself a loophole by saying they could have to adapt to cope with competition and forge European alliances.
His statement appeared framed not to rule out privatisation without alienating the Communist party, which holds the balance of power in parliament, and left-wingers in his Socialist party.

Socialist sources said public calls from such respected figures as Delors and Fiterman could help Jospin overcome resistance to selling stakes in state enterprises at a time when his government sorely needs the money.

Fiterman, who was transport minister from 1981 to 1984, did not go as far as to advocate full privatisation but said he had changed his mind from the days when he supported 100 percent state ownership.

"I think we have to get out of the religious debate over nationalisation versus privatisation," he told Liberation daily in an interview. "What matters is not the ownership structure but a strategy in the service of the company and the country."

For the airline to cope with international competition and increase its market share, "there is room for a diversification of the capital combining public control with a stake for the employees and participation by public or private companies with which Air France needs to work," Fiterman said.
The former transport minister went even further in heresy, in Communist eyes, by saying that even SNCF state railways should not be eternally unchanged.
"If we don't reform some companies, they risk being asphyxiated," he said.

On the other side, the French CNPF employers' association president Jean Gandois suggested on Sunday that the government could keep a "golden share" or a "blocking minority" to protect state interests in privatised defence and aerospace companies.
